feedback: If a child treats the fit alone as proof, ask: could two shapes fit by coincidence? What extra evidence makes it convincing? (matching fossils and rock bands crossing the seam).
If a child says Pangaea is 'just a guess', point to the independent evidence lines that agree: coastline fit, matching fossils/rocks across oceans, seafloor data, and the plate mechanism.
If a child imagines a fast or recent split, reconnect to the rate: a few cm per year adds up only over hundreds of millions of years, far longer than human history.

If a child treats the paper fit as exact proof, note that the real reconstruction uses continental-shelf edges and seafloor data, so the cut-out jigsaw is supporting evidence rather than the whole story.
activities.intendedInsight: The conclusion 'continents were once joined and have drifted apart' is a reasoned inference from converging evidence (coastline fit + matching fossils/rock + slow plate motion), not a just-so story or a single guess.
learnerActions: Cut out present-day continents (paper map) and move them around until the coastlines roughly fit together — notice South America nestling into Africa and how the pieces can be grouped into one approximate supercontinent (present-day coastlines and flat maps will leave gaps and overlaps).
Once assembled, overlay or draw on the areas of matching fossils (e.g. Mesosaurus, Glossopteris) and matching rock types so you can see them line up across the joins you just made.
State the inference in your own words: what do the puzzle-fit AND the matching fossils/rock together let you conclude, and why is each piece of evidence needed?
Estimate how long the break-up took if plates move only a few cm per year — relate that to 'hundreds of millions of years'.
Optionally, use a rotating globe (physical or digital) to rewind and watch the continents merge into Pangaea as a companion view of the same reassembly.
activities.title: Reassemble Pangaea, then check the evidence

feedback: If a child reasons 'hot lava → hotter world', redirect: the local heat is negligible globally; after a large sulphur-rich eruption, a high haze of tiny sulphur droplets spreads around the world, reflects sunlight and cools it for a while.
If a child thinks an eruption only affects the nearby area, use the ash-spread map: fine ash and gas travel on winds and reach far-away countries.

Reinforce that the cooling is temporary (months to a few years) and depends on how much sulphur gas is released and whether it reaches the stratosphere — explosive style sends material higher, which helps the effect spread globally.
activities.intendedInsight: Large explosive eruptions that put lots of sulphur gas into the stratosphere can affect global weather/climate: the gas forms tiny droplets that reflect sunlight, temporarily cooling the planet — an atmospheric mechanism distinct from local lava damage, while ash mostly affects the region it drifts over.
learnerActions: Pick a real eruption and trace how its ash cloud spread — e.g. map Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 ash creeping across Europe and grounding thousands of flights.

For a large explosive eruption, describe the chain: sulphur gas blasted high into the stratosphere forms a haze of tiny droplets that reflects sunlight, so less warmth reaches the surface and global temperatures can dip for months to a few years (most ash falls out within days to weeks).
Explain in writing or speech why the effect is COOLING, not warming, even though lava is hot — distinguish the tiny local heat from the global veil of sulphur droplets that reflects sunlight.
Contrast local devastation near the volcano (lava, blast, ashfall) with the GLOBAL effect carried through the atmosphere.
activities.title: How a single volcano reaches the whole planet

feedback: If a child treats all eruptions as identical, contrast a gentle lava flow with an explosive blast that sends ash into the high atmosphere.
Prompt learners to name which effects are local (blast, landslide) and which could be regional/global (high ash).
activities.intendedInsight: Eruption style governs both local reshaping and how far-reaching the effects are; explosive eruptions can loft material high enough to affect regions far from the volcano.
learnerActions: Compare before-and-after images of Mount St Helens (1980) and describe how the lateral blast reshaped the mountain.
Describe at least one key effect of this famous eruption, separating the immediate local destruction from any wider atmospheric effects.

Connect eruption STYLE to reach: explain why an explosive eruption throws ash and gas higher, and why material that reaches higher can travel farther (and, if it includes lots of sulphur gas, can cool the climate more widely).
activities.title: Study the before/after of a reshaped mountain

feedback: If the role-play stays at 'they just fit', the questioner should demand the independent evidence lines Wegener had (matching fossils/rock, signs of ancient glaciers); a modern-scientist character can add seafloor data and the plate mechanism, which were discovered after Wegener's death.
Use this as a complement to the hands-on reassembly: discussing the puzzle-fit does not itself give the child the physical construction, so pairing the two is suggested.
activities.intendedInsight: Scientific claims should be defended with evidence rather than asserted; voicing and challenging the reasoning out loud is intended to reinforce understanding of both the drift evidence and the global reach of eruptions.
learnerActions: Role-play or hold a discussion where one person takes the role of Alfred Wegener defending continental drift and must cite evidence (coastline fit, matching fossils/rock) when challenged.
Alternatively, interview a 'pilot grounded by Eyjafjallajökull ash' or a 'scientist at St Helens' to surface the human impact and the global reach of a single eruption.
Listeners ask follow-up questions that push for the mechanism, e.g. 'How do you KNOW they were joined?' or 'Why would ash so far away affect my flight?'
activities.title: Interview the scientist (optional spoken extension)
